newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Defence says genocide tribunal has no jurisdiction.
newsitem.headline: Defence says genocide tribunal has no jurisdiction.

text.p: Lawyers defending a Rwandan accused of genocide on Monday asked an international tribunal to dismiss a case against him, arguing it had no jurisdiction to try him.

Lawyers Evans Monari and Michelle Marchand, co-defending Joseph Kanyabashi, filed a 17-page motion to judges hearing the case at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda at Arusha, northern Tanzania.
The petition argued the tribunal, set up in November 1994, had no authority because it was not established by the U.N. General Assembly or an international treaty.

"The establishment of the tribunal by the (U.N.) Security Council was...ill-founded political action, not reasonably aimed at restoring and maintaining peace and bringing reconciliation to all the people of Rwanda," Monari said.
"If the overall aim is to establish peace and bring reconciliation...would it not be very likely that amnesty for those indicted would prove a more effective measure to achieve this aim?"
The court said it would rule on the petition by June 24.

The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda was modelled on the Hague-based criminal tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, which was set up by the United Nations in 1993 and was the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.
The Rwanda tribunal has been plagued by problems in attempting to bring to justice the leaders of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
So far 21 people have been indicted by the Rwanda tribunal, which has a total of 12 suspects in detention in Arusha.

Monari, whose client is accused of genocide, complicity in genocide and direct and public incitement to genocide, questioned the impartiality of the tribunal to judge those indicted because it did not take certain factors into account.

In particular, he said, the court was unable to review serious human rights violations committed against Hutus by the Tutsi-dominated Rwandan Patriotic Front, the rebel force which seized power to end the three-month genocide.

Monari added that the establishment of an international tribunal was ill-founded as there was no international conflict to warrant its creation. Instead, he said, it was set up by European and American countries concerned at a possible influx of refugees.
Prosecutor Yacob Haile-Mariam urged the court to dismiss the petition.
Although established by the U.N. Security Council, the tribunal's judges and prosecutors were appointed by the General Assembly.
Earlier this year the tribunal was the subject of a damning U.N. report, which accused it of incompetence and inefficiency.
